AIPE Sample Size Planning for a Fixed Effect in a Two-Level Mixed-Effects Model

Source: R/ss_aipe_mixed_effects.R
ss_aipe_mixed_effects.Rd

Computes the smallest number of clusters (i.e., Level 2 units) for which the confidence interval for the fixed-effect slope of one predictor has an expected full width no larger than width, in a balanced two-level model with a random intercept. The predictor may be measured on the individuals (i.e., Level 1) or on the clusters (i.e., Level 2), and may be centered at its cluster mean, centered at its grand mean, or left as it is. ss_aipe_mixed_effects_sensitivity simulates the same design, analysis, and interval, so the two can be used together: plan here, then check the plan there, including under values other than the ones planned with.

Usage

ss_aipe_mixed_effects(
  true_total_var,
  true_var_X,
  true_icc,
  width,
  cluster_size = 20L,
  conf_level = 0.95,
  predictor_level = 1,
  centering = c("cluster_mean", "grand_mean", "none"),
  true_icc_X = 0
)

Arguments

true_total_var

Population variance of the outcome given the predictor (a planning value): the variance of the random intercept (between clusters) plus the residual variance (within clusters). It is the name the total variance has in the cluster randomized planners (ss_aipe_crd).

true_var_X

Population variance of the predictor (a planning value). For an individual-level (i.e., Level 1) predictor it is the total variance over individuals, between and within clusters together (see true_icc_X); for a cluster-level (i.e., Level 2) predictor it is the variance over clusters.

true_icc

Population intraclass correlation of the outcome given the predictor (a planning value): the share of true_total_var that lies between clusters. In [0, 1).

width

Desired full width of the confidence interval for the slope.

cluster_size

Number of individuals (i.e., Level 1 units) in each cluster (i.e., Level 2 unit), the same in every cluster. Default 20L.

conf_level

Confidence level. Default 0.95.

predictor_level

1 (the default) for an individual-level predictor, which varies within a cluster, or 2 for a cluster-level predictor, which is the same for every individual of a cluster.

centering

How the predictor enters the model. "cluster_mean" (the default) subtracts each cluster's mean from its individuals' values, so the slope is the within-cluster slope; it applies to an individual-level predictor only. "grand_mean" subtracts the overall mean, and "none" leaves the predictor as it is. These two give the same slope and the same interval (only the intercept differs), and both are offered so that the call can say what the analysis will do.

true_icc_X

Population intraclass correlation of an individual-level predictor (a planning value): the share of true_var_X that lies between clusters. Default 0, a predictor whose cluster means differ by sampling alone. It is not used with predictor_level = 2.

Value

A data.frame with rows for the necessary number of clusters necessary_n_clusters, the implied total sample size total_N (necessary_n_clusters * cluster_size), the desired width, the expected_width at the necessary number of clusters, the degrees of freedom df of the interval's t quantile, and the inputs true_icc, true_icc_X, cluster_size, and predictor_level. The centering is recorded in attr(x, "centering").

Details

The model. For individual \(i\) of cluster \(k\), $$y_{ki} = \gamma_0 + \beta x_{ki} + u_k + e_{ki},$$ with \(u_k \sim N(0, \tau^2)\) the random intercept of the cluster and \(e_{ki} \sim N(0, \sigma^2)\) the residual of the individual, in \(K\) clusters of \(m\) individuals each. With \(V\) for true_total_var and \(\rho\) for true_icc, \(\tau^2 = \rho V\) and \(\sigma^2 = (1 - \rho) V\). The slope has the same value within and between clusters. Writing \(\sigma^2_X\) for true_var_X and \(\rho_X\) for true_icc_X, an individual-level predictor has variance \(\rho_X \sigma^2_X\) between clusters and \(\sigma^2_W = (1 - \rho_X)\sigma^2_X\) within them.

The interval planned for. The interval is \(\hat\beta \pm t_{1 - \alpha/2,\, \nu}\, \widehat{SE}(\hat\beta)\), with \(\nu = K(m - 1) - 1\) for an individual-level predictor and \(\nu = K - 2\) for a cluster-level predictor (the regression of \(K\) cluster means). Its expected width is \(2\, t_{1 - \alpha/2,\, \nu}\, E[\widehat{SE}(\hat\beta)]\), and the function returns the smallest \(K\) at which that is no larger than width. No value of the slope is needed: \(\beta\) does not appear in any of the expressions below.

The expected standard error. Each expression follows from the sums of squares of a balanced design.

  • Individual-level predictor centered at its cluster mean. The estimate is the within-cluster slope, and for a normally distributed predictor the expected standard error is exactly $$E[\widehat{SE}(\hat\beta)] = \frac{\sigma}{\sigma_W \sqrt{K (m - 1) - 1}}.$$ Clustering of the outcome enters only through \(\sigma\): the design effect \(1 + (m - 1)\rho\) that inflates the variance of a cluster-level quantity does not appear, because centering removes the differences among clusters from both variables.

  • Cluster-level predictor. The estimate is the slope of the regression of the cluster means of the outcome on the predictor, and for a normally distributed predictor the expected standard error is exactly $$E[\widehat{SE}(\hat\beta)] = \frac{\sqrt{\tau^2 + \sigma^2 / m}}{\sigma_X \sqrt{K - 2}}.$$ Here the number of clusters is what buys precision: as \(m\) grows the numerator approaches \(\tau\) and not 0.

  • Individual-level predictor centered at its grand mean, or not centered. The estimate pools the within-cluster and the between-cluster information about the one slope, each weighted by its precision, and to first order $$E[\widehat{SE}(\hat\beta)]^2 \approx \left[ \frac{\{K (m - 1) - 1\}\, \sigma^2_W}{\sigma^2} + \frac{(K - 2)\,(\rho_X \sigma^2_X + \sigma^2_W / m)} {\tau^2 + \sigma^2 / m} \right]^{-1},$$ which reduces to the two expressions above when either part is absent. It is never larger than the value for the within-cluster slope, and the gain is what the assumption of one slope within and between clusters buys; when that assumption is in doubt, plan for the cluster-mean-centered analysis.

In 4,000 simulated data sets for each of six designs (clusters of 5 to 20, 9 to 44 clusters, intraclass correlations of .05 to .30), the mean width of the interval was within 0.3 percent of the expected width in the four designs with an exact expression, and 0.5 and 1.3 percent narrower than it in the two with a pooled slope, so the first-order expression errs toward a slightly larger number of clusters. ss_aipe_mixed_effects_sensitivity reports the mean width and the coverage for any design.

Scope. One predictor, a random intercept, a fixed slope, and clusters of equal size. For random slopes, cross-level interactions, or unequal cluster sizes the variance changes and a Monte Carlo planner should be used (Schoemann, Boulton, & Short, 2017). The two-level random-intercept model is treated at length by Snijders and Bosker (2012).

References

Schoemann, A. M., Boulton, A. J., & Short, S. D. (2017). Determining power and sample size for simple and complex mediation models. Social Psychological and Personality Science, 8(4), 379–386. doi:10.1177/1948550617715068

Snijders, T. A. B., & Bosker, R. J. (2012). Multilevel analysis: An introduction to basic and advanced multilevel modeling (2nd ed.). Sage.

Examples

# 1. An individual-level predictor centered at its cluster mean (the
#    default): clusters of 20, intraclass correlation .10, unit
#    variances, and a desired width of .20.
ss_aipe_mixed_effects(true_total_var = 1, true_var_X = 1, true_icc = 0.10,
                      width = 0.20, cluster_size = 20)
#>  term                 value
#>  necessary_n_clusters 19   
#>  total_N              380  
#>  width                0.200
#>  expected_width       0.197
#>  df                   360  
#>  true_icc             0.100
#>  true_icc_X           0    
#>  cluster_size         20   
#>  predictor_level      1    
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 2. The same predictor not centered, when 30 percent of its variance
#    lies between clusters.
ss_aipe_mixed_effects(true_total_var = 1, true_var_X = 1, true_icc = 0.10,
                      width = 0.20, cluster_size = 20,
                      centering = "none", true_icc_X = 0.30)
#>  term                 value
#>  necessary_n_clusters 23   
#>  total_N              460  
#>  width                0.200
#>  expected_width       0.200
#>  df                   436  
#>  true_icc             0.100
#>  true_icc_X           0.300
#>  cluster_size         20   
#>  predictor_level      1    
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%

# 3. A cluster-level predictor: far more clusters are needed for the
#    same width, because each cluster supplies one value of it.
ss_aipe_mixed_effects(true_total_var = 1, true_var_X = 1, true_icc = 0.10,
                      width = 0.20, cluster_size = 20,
                      predictor_level = 2, centering = "grand_mean")
#>  term                 value
#>  necessary_n_clusters 61   
#>  total_N              1220 
#>  width                0.200
#>  expected_width       0.198
#>  df                   59   
#>  true_icc             0.100
#>  true_icc_X           0    
#>  cluster_size         20   
#>  predictor_level      2    
#> 
#> Confidence level: 95%
